items: 1Define matrices and their special types — square, null/zero, identity and singular matrices — and state a matrix's order.
2Add, subtract, multiply and transpose matrices, and apply the properties of scalar multiplication and transposition.
3Compute determinants of 2×2 and 3×3 matrices by cofactor expansion, and apply the key properties of determinants.

5Solve systems of linear equations using Cramer's Rule, expressing the system first in matrix form AX = b.

blocks.x: Matrix A rectangular array of numbers arranged in rows and columns. The numbers in a matrix are called its elements/entries.
Order The order (dimension) of a matrix is the number of rows by the number of columns, e.g. a 2×3 matrix has 2 rows and 3 columns.
Identity matrix A square matrix with 1s on the leading diagonal and 0s everywhere else. It is called the "unit" matrix because AI = A for any conformable matrix A.
Singular matrix A square matrix A is singular (non-invertible) whenever |A| = 0, since A-1 = (1/|A|)·Adj(A) is undefined in that case.
Matrix basics→ Operations→ Determinants→ Inverse→ Cramer's Rule

c: Same number of rows as columns
1s on leading diagonal, 0s elsewhere; AI = A
Square matrix with |A| = 0 — has no inverse

blocks.x: Matrices, their special types, and the four core operations: addition, subtraction, multiplication and transposition.
Has the same number of rows as columns, e.g. [1 2 3; 4 5 6; 3 3 7] and [1 2; 4 5] are both square.
A matrix in which every element is zero, e.g. [0 0; 0 0] or a 3×3 matrix of all zeros.
A square matrix whose leading diagonal is all 1s and every other entry is 0. Any matrix multiplied by I gives the same matrix: AI = A.
A square matrix A is singular if |A| = 0. Since A<sup>-1</sup> = (1/|A|)Adj(A), A has no inverse whenever |A| = 0.
Two matrices can be added only if they are of the same order. Corresponding elements are added: [a b; c d] + [e f; g h] = [a+e b+f; c+g d+h].

items: 1Add each entry of A to the corresponding entry of B.A+B = [3+10 4+6; 9+7 1+5]
2Simplify each entry.A+B = [13 10; 16 6]

blocks.x: As with addition, two matrices can be subtracted only if they are of the same dimension.
For A = [3 4; 9 1] and B = [10 6; 7 5], find A − B.

items: 1Subtract each entry of B from the corresponding entry of A.A−B = [3−10 4−6; 9−7 1−5]
2Simplify each entry.A−B = [−7 −2; 2 −4]

blocks.x: Matrices A and B can only be multiplied if the number of columns of A equals the number of rows of B. An (m×n) matrix times an (n×p) matrix gives an (m×p) matrix: [a b; c d]×[e f; g h] = [ae+bg af+bh; ce+dg cf+dh].
For A = [3 4; 9 1] and B = [10 6; 7 5], find AB.

items: 1Multiply each row of A by each column of B.AB = [3(10)+4(7) 3(6)+4(5); 9(10)+1(7) 9(6)+1(5)]
2Simplify each entry.AB = [58 38; 97 59]

blocks.x: Remark If A and B are conformable matrices, AB ≠ BA in general — matrix multiplication is not commutative. If α is a scalar, αA scales every entry of A by α.
The transpose switches the rows and columns of a matrix. If A has dimension m×n, then A<sup>T</sup> has dimension n×m: mathematically, if A = [a<sub>ij</sub>] then A<sup>T</sup> = [a<sub>ji</sub>].

items: 1Row 1 of A becomes column 1 of A<sup>T</sup>.(2, 1, 4) → column 1
2Row 2 of A becomes column 2, and row 3 becomes column 3.(3, 5, 0) → col 2 (7, 3, 9) → col 3
1A matrix A is symmetric if its transpose equals itself: AT = A.
2(A + B)<sup>T</sup> = A<sup>T</sup> + B<sup>T</sup>
3(αA)<sup>T</sup> = αA<sup>T</sup>
4(AB)<sup>T</sup> = B<sup>T</sup>A<sup>T</sup> — note the order reverses.

blocks.x: The determinant of a square matrix A, written det(A) or |A|, is a scalar value that is a function of A's entries.

|A| for a 2×2 matrix
For A = [a b; c d], the determinant is defined as |A| = ad − bc.

items: 1Apply |A| = ad − bc, multiplying the two diagonals.det(T) = (4×9) − (10×5)
2Simplify.det(T) = 36 − 50

blocks.x:
|A| for a 3×3 matrix
For A = [a b c; d e f; g h i], expand along the first row: |A| = a|e f; h i| − b|d f; g i| + c|d e; g h|.

items: 1Expand along the first row, alternating signs (+, −, +).|A| = 3|2 5; 6 3| − 8|0 5; 4 3| + 7|0 2; 4 6|
3Simplify each bracket.= 3(−24) − 8(−20) + 7(−8)
4Combine the terms.= −72 + 160 − 56
1The determinant of the identity matrix is 1.
2Interchanging any two rows/columns of a square matrix multiplies its determinant by −1.
3Multiplying a row/column by a scalar multiplies the determinant by the same scalar.
4The determinant is unchanged if rows and columns are interchanged: |A| = |A<sup>T</sup>|.
5If all elements in a row/column are zero, the determinant is zero.
6If any two rows/columns are identical, the determinant is zero.

blocks.x: A square matrix A has an inverse A⁻¹ such that AA⁻¹ = A⁻¹A = I. Getting there means working through minors, cofactors and the adjoint.
Minor, Mij The determinant of the submatrix left after deleting the row and column that the element aij lies on.

Cofactor, C<sub>ij</sub>
The determinant of the minor for that element, multiplied by +1 or −1 depending on position: C<sub>ij</sub> = (−1)<sup>i+j</sup>|M<sub>ij</sub>|.
Adjoint, Adj(A) The transpose of the matrix of cofactors of A.

Formula
For A = [a b; c d], A<sup>-1</sup> = (1/det(A))·[d −b; −c a], where det(A) = ad − bc.
Given A = [1 6; 4 5], find the inverse of A.

items: 1Find the determinant.det(A) = 5(1) − 4(6) = −19
2Swap a and d, negate b and c, then divide by det(A).A<sup>-1</sup> = −119 [5 −6; −4 1]
3Distribute the scalar into each entry.A<sup>-1</sup> = [−5/19 6/19; 4/19 −1/19]

blocks.x: Steps: 1. Find the determinant of the given matrix. 2. Find the matrix of cofactors. 3. Transpose the matrix of cofactors to get the adjoint. 4. Divide each term of the adjoint by the determinant.

items: 2Find the minor for each of the 9 entries. First row:|1 4; 6 0|=−24, |0 4; 5 0|=−20, |0 1; 5 6|=−5
5Apply the checkerboard sign (−1)<sup>i+j</sup> to get the matrix of cofactors.Cofactors = [−24 20 −5; 18 −15 4; 5 −4 1]
6Transpose the cofactor matrix to get the adjoint.Adj(A) = [−24 18 5; 20 −15 −4; −5 4 1]
7Divide by det(A) = 1 (so A<sup>-1</sup> equals the adjoint here).A<sup>-1</sup> = (1/1)·Adj(A)

sections.title: Writing a system in matrix form

blocks.x: Matrices can solve systems of simultaneous equations. This module covers Cramer's Rule, a method that uses determinants; Gaussian Elimination is the other method mentioned.
Writing a system in matrix form

A system of n = 3 linear equations in 3 variables, a1x+b1y+c1z=α, a2x+b2y+c2z=β, a3x+b3y+c3z=γ, can be written as AX = b, where A is the 3×3 coefficient matrix, X the column vector of unknowns, and b the column vector of constants. The system has a unique solution when |A| ≠ 0, which is exactly when Cramer's Rule can be applied.

Cramer's Rule
x = |A<sub>1</sub>|/|A|, y = |A<sub>2</sub>|/|A|, z = |A<sub>3</sub>|/|A|, where A<sub>i</sub> is A with column i replaced by b.

items: 1Write A, X and b, then find det(A).A = [3 4; 1 −2], |A| = 3(−2) − 1(4) = −10
2Form A₁ by replacing column 1 of A with b = [6; 3], then find x₁.x₁ = |6 4; 3 −2| / |A| = [(−12)−(12)] / (−10) = −24/−10
3Simplify x₁.x₁ = 12/5
4Form A₂ by replacing column 2 of A with b, then find x₂.x₂ = |3 6; 1 3| / |A| = [(9)−(6)] / (−10) = 3/−10
